Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer **It’s not a bug – it’s the intended “local-fonts” fallback that MapLibre GL JS uses when the style has no `glyphs` URL.** When `glyphs` is omitted, GL JS falls back to rendering every label with the browser’s text engine (TinySDF) instead of fetching SDF glyph PBFs. The `text-font` array is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list: 1. **If the named font is already available on the device** (system font) → it is used. 2. **If you have added a web-font with `@font-face` (or `font-faces` in the style)** → the browser will download that file and use it. 3. **If the font cannot be found** → the browser picks its own generic fallback (usually “sans-serif”), which is why you see a “generic” look. So the map is working as designed; the only thing missing is **making the font you asked for actually reachable to the browser**. --- ## What’s really happening under the hood | Step | What MapLibre does | Result you see | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Style parsing** | No `glyphs` field → “local-fonts mode”. | No request for `…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`. | | **Label layout** | `text-font` is read as a *fallback list* of font-family names. | Same order you would write in CSS. | | **Font resolution** | 1. Look for a matching **`font-faces` entry** in the style (GL JS ≥ 6.7).
2. If none, ask the browser to resolve the name via normal CSS rules (`@font-face`, system fonts, `document.fonts`). | If the font is found → it is used.
If not → the browser falls back to its default sans-serif. | | **Glyph rendering** | For each glyph GL JS either:
• Uses the downloaded web-font (via the browser’s text rasterizer) **or**
• Generates an SDF on-the-fly with TinySDF (the same code path used for CJK ideographs). | Text appears, but possibly in a different typeface than you expected. | | **Logging** | When a glyph PBF would have been needed but can’t be loaded, GL JS logs a message like:
`Unable to load glyph range … Rendering codepoint U+XXXX locally instead.` | Helpful for debugging when you *do* have a `glyphs` URL that is broken. | > **Important:** This local-fonts fallback exists **only in MapLibre GL JS**. > MapLibre Native (Android / iOS / Qt) still requires a valid `glyphs` URL; omitting it will cause the layer to be invisible or throw an error. --- ## Why you’re seeing a *generic* font 1. **The font isn’t loaded at all** – you referenced `"My Fancy Font"` in `text-font`, but the browser never fetched a matching `@font-face` rule or `font-faces` entry. 2. **Name mismatch** – the name in `text-font` must match **exactly** the family name declared in the font file (or the `font-family` you set in `@font-face`). 3. **CORS / URL problems** – if you use `font-faces` and the `url` points to a cross-origin resource that blocks the request, the browser discards it and falls back. 4. **Weight/Style keywords** – `text-font` can contain a weight keyword (`"Bold"`). If you only supplied a regular-weight file, the browser may fall back to a generic bold system font. --- ## How to make the intended font appear ### 1. Load the font in the page (web-font approach) ```html ``` *Then* in your style: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ``` The browser will download the font, and GL JS will render labels with it. ### 2. Use the style-level `font-faces` property (GL JS ≥ 6.7) If you prefer to keep everything inside the style JSON (useful for offline bundles or when you want to change fonts at runtime): ```json { "font-faces": { "My Fancy Font": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-FFFF"] // optional, can be omitted } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["My Fancy Font", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ] } ``` You can also change it later with the API: ```js map.setFontFaces({ "My Fancy Font": [ { url: "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf" } ] }); ``` ### 3. Verify the name matches the font’s internal family name Open the TTF/OTF in a font-viewer (e.g., FontForge, macOS Font Book) and check the **Family Name** field. That exact string must appear in `text-font`. If the file contains multiple families (e.g., “My Fancy Font Regular” and “My Fancy Font Bold”), you can reference the weight keyword: ```json "text-font": ["My Fancy Font Bold", "My Fancy Font"] ``` or rely on the `font-weight` layout property. ### 4. Check CORS / MIME types - Serve the font with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) if it’s on a different origin. - Use a proper MIME type (`font/ttf`, `font/woff2`, etc.) so the browser accepts it. ### 5. Test in the console ```js document.fonts.load('1rem "My Fancy Font"').then(() => { console.log('Font loaded'); }); ``` If the promise never resolves, the browser couldn’t find the font. --- ## When you *don’t* need to do any of the above If you’re happy with the generic system font (or with the TinySDF-generated CJK fallback) you can leave the style as-is. The map will continue to work, but the visual identity of your labels will differ across browsers/OSes. --- ## TL;DR checklist | ✅ | Action | |---|--------| | ✅ | **Confirm you really want a custom font** – otherwise keep the default. | | ✅ | **Add a `@font-face` rule** (or a `font-faces` entry) that points to a reachable font file. | | ✅ | **Make sure the family name in `text-font` matches the font’s internal name** exactly. | | ✅ | **Serve the font with correct CORS headers** if it’s cross-origin. | | ✅ | **Reload the page** – you should now see the intended typeface. | | ❌ | If you omit all of the above, GL JS will fall back to a generic system font – this is expected behavior, not a bug. | --- ## Gotchas & extra notes | Situation | What to watch for | |-----------|-------------------| | **CJK characters** | Even with a `font-faces` entry, GL JS still uses the `localIdeographFontFamily` path (TinySDF) by default. Set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` **only** if you really need the served glyph shapes. | | **Right-to-left scripts (Arabic, Hebrew)** | Since GL JS 6.9 the engine shapes them automatically; you just need the font available. No `setRTLTextPlugin` required. | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, etc.** | These scripts are now rendered as grapheme clusters by the browser, so the glyph PBFs are ignored. Use `font-faces` (or a web-font) to control the appearance. | | **MapLibre Native** | You **must** provide a `glyphs` URL; the local-fonts fallback does not exist. If you need the same look on both platforms, keep a `glyphs` URL and also add `font-faces` for the scripts that need shaping. | | **Multiple fonts in the fallback list** | The first font that the browser can resolve is used for the whole label; you cannot mix fonts within a single label. | | **Weight/italic keywords** | `"Bold"` or `"Italic"` after the family name are interpreted as weight/style, not as separate family names. Ensure the font file you serve contains the requested weight/style, or the browser will synthesize it (often resulting in a generic look). | --- ### Bottom line - **No `glyphs` → local-fonts mode → browser decides the actual typeface.** - **If you want a specific font, you must make that font available to the browser** (via `@font-face` or `font-faces`). - **Everything you’re seeing is expected; it’s not a MapLibre bug.** Fix the font loading, and the labels will render exactly as you specified. Happy mapping!

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?

## TL;DR *MapLibre Native on Android **cannot** run without a `glyphs` URL.* What you can do is keep the `glyphs` field pointing at a **local file URL** (or a tiny on-device HTTP server) that serves the pre-generated glyph-PBFs **or even empty PBFs**. Then use the **`font-faces`** property to map every `text-font` name you use to a **bundled TTF/OTF** that lives in your app’s `assets/` (or `res/raw/`). All scripts that need shaping (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, etc.) will be drawn from those local font files via HarfBuzz; CJK characters will be drawn from the same local font (or, if you prefer, you can let the tiny-SDF fallback do it, but Native does not have the GL-JS “local-ideograph” shortcut). Below is a step-by-step recipe, plus the minimal style JSON you need. --- ## 1. Why a `glyphs` URL is still required | SDK | Behaviour when `glyphs` is missing | |-----|--------------------------------------| | **MapLibre GL JS** (≥ 5.11) | Falls back to the browser’s TinySDF renderer – you can omit `glyphs` completely. | | **MapLibre Native** (Android) | **Fails** – the style is considered invalid and the map will not render. The native code always tries to fetch a glyph PBF for every range that appears in a `text-font`.
*(Issue #165 is still open.)* | Therefore the *only* way to stay offline on Native is to give the style a **valid URL template** that resolves to something the SDK can read. The easiest offline solution is a **file-URL** that points at assets bundled with the APK. > **Bottom line:** you cannot “just omit `glyphs`”. You must supply a URL, but that URL can point at files that live inside the app package. --- ## 2. Bundle the needed font files 1. **Pick the fonts** you want to use. *For a world map the safest choice is the Noto family* (Noto Sans, Noto Sans CJK SC, Noto Sans Arabic, Noto Sans Devanagari, …). 2. **Copy the `.ttf`/`.otf` files** into `app/src/main/assets/fonts/`. ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ └─ assets/ └─ fonts/ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf └─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf ``` 3. (Optional) If you also want to keep the classic glyph-PBF route for Latin or other scripts, **pre-generate** the PBFs and drop them under `assets/glyphs/` using the same folder layout that a remote glyph server expects: ``` assets/ └─ glyphs/ └─ Noto%20Sans/ ├─ 0-255.pbf ├─ 256-511.pbf └─ … ``` *You can generate those PBFs with the online tool **Font Maker** (https://maplibre.github.io/font-maker/) or with `fontnik`.* --- ## 3. Add a `font-faces` block to your style The `font-faces` property tells both GL JS **and** Native how to resolve a `text-font` name to a concrete font file on the device. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] // Latin, Latin-Extended } ], "Noto Sans CJK SC": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKSC-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"] // CJK Unified Ideographs } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": [ "Noto Sans CJK SC", "Noto Sans Arabic", "Noto Sans Devanagari", "Noto Sans Regular" ], "text-size": 12 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` ### What the block does | Property | Meaning | |----------|---------| | `url` (file URL) | Points at a font file that the Android runtime can read directly from the APK. | | `unicode-range` | Limits the font to the code-points you list. Anything outside falls back to the next entry in the `text-font` list, or finally to the glyph-PBFs (if they exist). | | `text-font` list in the layer | Acts like a CSS fallback list. The first entry whose `unicode-range` covers the character(s) wins. | > **Tip:** If you *don’t* bundle any glyph-PBFs, you can set the `glyphs` URL to a **dummy path** that always returns a 204 (empty body). The SDK will still try to fetch it, but the request will be instantaneous and the text will be drawn from the `font-faces` files you supplied. --- ## 4. Configure the Android MapLibre Native client ```kotlin import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibreMapOptions import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style val options = MapLibreMapOptions.createFromAttributes(this, null).apply { // Point at the same file-URL you used in the style JSON. glyphsUrl("file:///android_asset/glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf") // (Optional) If you want to use a custom local CJK font for ideographs, // you can set the same font-family here – Native does not have a // `localIdeographFontFamily` option, so just rely on `font-faces`. } // Create the map view val mapView = MapView(this, options) setContentView(mapView) // Load the style (the JSON above, stored in assets/style.json) mapView.getMapAsync { maplibreMap -> maplibreMap.setStyle( Style.Builder().fromUri("asset://style.json") ) } ``` ### Important notes * **File-URL syntax** – Android’s `AssetManager` understands `file:///android_asset/…`. The glyph-PBFs for these scripts are **ignored** when a matching `font-faces` entry exists. | | **Mixed-script labels** | The `text-font` list order decides which font wins for each character. Description: anti-pattern — porting a Native font-faces config to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## Short answer  

**Yes – you can reuse the same `font-faces` block in a MapLibre GL JS style, but you have to meet a few extra requirements that only exist in the browser:**

| What you already have (Native) | What you must add / check for GL JS |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `font-faces` entries that point at **local files** on the device (e.g. `file:///…/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf`). | The URLs must be **fetchable over HTTP(S)** by the browser (or be data-URIs). A plain file-system path will not work. |
| Unicode-range filters are already in the spec. | No change – GL JS reads the same `unicode-range` array. |
| Native automatically uses those files for shaping (HarfBuzz). | GL JS will also use them, but only for the scripts that are **drawn by the browser** (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, etc.). For Latin-style scripts you still need a glyph-PBF source **unless you rely on the new local-font fallback** (GL JS ≥ 5.11.0). |
| Offline-only – the app ships the font files with the binary. | You must **serve the font files** (e.g. from your web server, a CDN, or a Service-Worker cache) so the browser can download them the first time. After that they can be cached for offline use. |
| No need for `map.setFontFaces()` at runtime. | If you want to change the mapping after the map is created you can call `map.setFontFaces()`; otherwise the static `font-faces` block is enough. |

Below is a step-by-step checklist and a minimal example that shows exactly how to copy the Native config into a GL JS style and make it work offline.

---

## 1️⃣ Make sure you are on a recent GL JS version  

* `font-faces` support was added in **v6.7.0**.  
* The **local-font fallback** (no `glyphs` URL or failed glyph fetch) landed in **v5.11.0**.  

If you are using an older version, upgrade first:

```bash
npm install maplibre-gl@^6.15.0   # latest stable at time of writing
```

---

## 2️⃣ Keep the `font-faces` block exactly as you have it  

Native and GL JS read the same JSON structure, e.g.:

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [
    /* … your symbol layers that use text-font … */
  ]
}
```

> **Copy-paste** the whole `font-faces` object into the GL JS style file. No syntax changes are needed.

---

## 3️⃣ Serve the font files over HTTP(S)

The browser cannot read `file:///…` URLs, so you must make the `.ttf/.otf` files reachable via a normal web request.

### Options

| Option | How to do it | Offline-caching notes |
|--------|--------------|------------------------|
| **Static web server** (e.g. `public/fonts/…` in a Vite/Next/CRA app) | Place the files in the public folder; reference them with a relative URL (`/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf`). | The browser will cache them automatically (Cache-Control headers). |
| **CDN / third-party host** | Upload the files to a CDN and use the CDN URL. | Same caching rules as any other asset. |
| **Service Worker** | Intercept the fetch for the font URL and serve a pre-bundled `ArrayBuffer` (or a data-URI). | Guarantees offline availability even if the user never visited the page while online. |
| **Data URI** (base64-encoded) | Replace the `url` value with `data:font/ttf;base64,…`. | Works offline out-of-the-box, but the style file becomes huge. Use only for very small fonts. |

> **CORS** – If you host the fonts on a different origin, make sure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). Otherwise the browser will block the request and fall back to the generic system font.

---

## 4️⃣ Decide whether you still need a `glyphs` URL

### Scenario A – You **do not** need any glyph-PBFs  

*If you are happy with the browser-drawn text for *all* scripts* (Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic, Devanagari, etc.) you can **omit the `glyphs` field entirely**.  

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "font-faces": { … },
  "layers": [ … ]
}
```

* GL JS will treat every `text-font` entry as a CSS-style font-family list and render everything locally with TinySDF (for ideographs) or the browser’s shaping engine (for complex scripts).  
* This is the **offline-first** mode – no network request for glyph PBFs will ever be made.

### Scenario B – You still want **glyph PBFs for Latin/Western scripts**  

* Keep the `glyphs` URL (e.g. the OpenMapTiles font server).  
* GL JS will request the PBFs for the ranges that are **not covered** by any `font-faces` entry **or** that are not part of a script that the browser draws itself.  
* If a request fails (404, CORS, offline), GL JS falls back to the local-font path automatically (since v5.11.0). So you still get a graceful offline experience.

---

## 5️⃣ (Optional) Change the mapping at runtime  

If you need to swap a font after the map is already created (e.g. user selects a different language), call:

```js
map.setFontFaces({
  "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
    {
      url: "/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
      "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
    }
  ],
  // … other faces …
});
```

`setFontFaces` replaces the whole `font-faces` object; it does **not** merge with the existing one.

---

## 6️⃣ Special cases you still need to be aware of

| Script | How GL JS draws it | What you must provide |
|--------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| **CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean)** | Rendered **locally** by default via `localIdeographFontFamily` (TinySDF). `text-font` is ignored except for weight. | No glyph PBFs needed. If you *do* want the exact shapes from a server-served font, set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` in the map options (but this is slower and usually unnecessary). |
| **Arabic / Hebrew** | Shaped by the browser from version 6.9.0 onward; no RTL plugin needed. | Just list the appropriate Noto font in `text-font` and provide it via `font-faces`. |
| **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | Drawn as **grapheme clusters** by the browser (since GL JS 6.15.0). Glyph PBFs are ignored. | Provide the script-specific TTF/OTF via `font-faces` (as you already do). |
| **Latin, Greek, Cyrillic** | If you have a `glyphs` URL, GL JS will request PBFs; otherwise it falls back to the local-font path. | Either keep the glyph server *or* omit `glyphs` and rely on the local fallback. |

---

## 7️⃣ Full example – offline-first GL JS style

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "name": "Offline demo",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
      {
        "url": "/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [
      {
        "url": "/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF"]
      }
    ],
    "Noto Sans Regular": [
      {
        "url": "/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"]
      }
    ]
  },
  // No glyphs field → pure local-font mode
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular",
          "Noto Sans Arabic Regular",
          "Noto Sans Regular"
        ],
        "text-size": 14
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

*Place the JSON in `style.json`, serve the three `.ttf` files from `/fonts/`, and initialise the map:*

```js
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: '/style.json',
  center: [77.2, 28.6],
  zoom: 10,
  // optional: change the on-device CJK font
  localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif'
});
```

When the user first loads the page, the three font files are fetched once, cached by the browser, and thereafter the map works **completely offline** (no glyph PBF requests, no RTL plugin, no extra network traffic).

---

## TL;DR checklist for copying `font-faces` from Native to GL JS

1. **Upgrade GL JS to ≥ 6.7.0** (or ≥ 5.11.0 if you only need the fallback).  
2. **Copy the `font-faces` block verbatim** into the GL JS style.  
3. **Make every `url` reachable over HTTP(S)** (static server, CDN, Service Worker, or data-URI).  
4. **Add CORS headers** if the fonts are on a different origin.  
5. **Decide whether you need a `glyphs` URL**:  
   * Omit it for a fully offline, local-font-only map.  
   * Keep it if you still want PBFs for Latin/Western scripts.  
6. (Optional) Call `map.setFontFaces()` if you need to modify the mapping after map creation.  
7. Test offline: open the page, let the fonts load once, then disable the network and reload – the labels should still appear.

If you follow those steps, the offline-font behavior you have in MapLibre Native will be reproduced in your MapLibre GL JS web app. Happy mapping!

prompt: My MapLibre GL JS 6 map has Arabic and Hebrew place names. What do I need to set up so those labels read right-to-left with the Arabic letters joined correctly?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR | What you need | How to do it | |---------------|--------------| | **MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.9.0** (the version you already have) | No extra plugin – the engine now shapes Arabic/Hebrew itself. | | **A font that contains the Arabic/Hebrew glyphs** (e.g. *Noto Sans Arabic* / *Noto Sans Hebrew*) | Add the font name to every layer that draws place-name text (`text-font`). | | **A `glyphs` URL or `font-faces` entry** that points at the same font (or rely on the GL-JS local-font fallback) | Either keep the style’s `glyphs` pointing at a glyph-PBF server **or** omit `glyphs` and let GL JS load the font locally. | | **`text-direction: "right-to-left"`** (optional – GL JS will infer it from the script) | Set it on the layer if you want to force RTL for mixed-script labels. | | **(If you ever run an older GL JS < 6.9.0)** | Load the RTL-text plugin **once**, before creating the map. | Below is a step-by-step guide that covers the *current* way (GL JS ≥ 6.9.0) and also shows the legacy fallback for older versions. --- ## 1. Verify you are really on GL JS ≥ 6.9.0 ```js import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; console.log('MapLibre version →', maplibregl.version); // Should print something like "6.9.0" or newer. ``` If the version is **6.9.0** or later you can skip the RTL-plugin entirely. If you are stuck on an older version (e.g. 6.7.0) read the *Legacy* section at the end. --- ## 2. Choose a font that supports Arabic & Hebrew The easiest, free, and most widely-used choice is Google’s **Noto** family: | Script | Font name (as used in `text-font`) | Example URL for the TTF (if you need `font-faces`) | |--------|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------| | Arabic | `"Noto Sans Arabic Regular"` | `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` | | Hebrew | `"Noto Sans Hebrew Regular"` | `https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf` | > **Why Noto?** It covers the whole Unicode range for those scripts, is open-source, and is already bundled in the public `demotiles.maplibre.org/font` glyph server. ### 2-a. Using a **glyph-PBF server** (the classic way) If you already have a `glyphs` URL (e.g. `https://mytiles.example.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) you only need to make sure the **folder names** match the `text-font` strings exactly. ``` /font/ Noto%20Sans%20Arabic%20Regular/ 0-255.pbf 256-511.pbf … Noto%20Sans%20Hebrew%20Regular/ 0-255.pbf … ``` > **Tip:** The OpenMapTiles `fonts` repo already contains the pre-built PBFs for all Noto fonts. You can copy that tree to your own origin and point `glyphs` at it. ### 2-b. **Local-font fallback** (no glyph server needed) Since **GL JS 5.11.0** you can *omit* the `glyphs` property entirely. The engine will load the fonts you list in `text-font` via normal web-font loading (`@font-face` or `document.fonts.load`). This is handy for offline or self-hosted apps. ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": null, // <-- omit or set to null "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Arabic Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF", "U+FB50-FDFF", "U+FE70-FEFF", "U+1EE00-1EEFF"] } ], "Noto Sans Hebrew Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansHebrew-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0590-05FF", "U+FB1D-FB4F"] } ] }, "layers": [ … ] } ``` > **Important:** The URLs must be reachable from the browser (CORS-enabled, HTTPS, etc.). If you are serving the fonts from the same origin as the page you can use relative URLs. --- ## 3. Add the font to your text layers Every layer that draws place-name labels (`symbol` layers with a `text-field`) needs a `text-font` array that includes the Arabic/Hebrew font **as the first entry** (or at least before any generic fallback). Example: ```json { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"], "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], // assumes the OSM name is already in Arabic/Hebrew "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", // try Arabic first "Noto Sans Hebrew Regular", // then Hebrew "Noto Sans Regular", // generic fallback for Latin, etc. "Open Sans Regular" ], "text-size": 12, "text-allow-overlap": false, "text-anchor": "center", "text-justify": "auto", // optional; GL JS will auto-detect direction "text-direction": "right-to-left" // optional – forces RTL even if script detection fails }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` ### Why the order matters * `text-font` works like CSS `font-family`: the first font that contains the needed glyphs is used. * For Arabic text you want the Arabic-specific Noto font first; otherwise the engine may fall back to a Latin font that has no Arabic shaping and you’ll see disconnected letters. --- ## 4. Let the engine handle right-to-left shaping ### 4-a. Modern GL JS (≥ 6.9.0) *No extra code is required.* The engine automatically: 1. Detects that the code points belong to an RTL script. 2. Shapes the characters with the correct joining forms (lam-alef ligatures, etc.). 3. Renders the glyphs in the correct visual order. If you have mixed-script labels (e.g. Arabic + Latin), you can force the whole string to be treated as RTL with the `text-direction` property shown above, or you can let the engine infer it per-character (the default works for most cases). ### 4-b. Legacy GL JS (< 6.9.0) If you ever need to support an older version, you must load the **RTL-text plugin** *once* **before** creating the map: ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; // Load the plugin from a CDN or your own copy. setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/@mapbox/mapbox-gl-rtl-text@0.3.0/dist/mapbox-gl-rtl-text.js', /* lazy */ false // true = load on-demand; false = load now (recommended for first-load) ); ``` After the plugin is registered, create the map as usual. The plugin will be used internally for Arabic/Hebrew shaping. > **Note:** The plugin is **deprecated** and will be removed in a future major release. Upgrading to GL JS ≥ 6.9.0 is the recommended long-term solution. --- ## 5. Verify that the text looks correct 1. **Open the map in the browser** and zoom to a place that has an Arabic or Hebrew name (e.g. “القاهرة” or “תל אביב”). 2. **Inspect the label** with the browser’s dev-tools → Elements → Computed → `font-family`. It should show the Noto font you specified. 3. **Check the direction**: the characters should be joined (lam-alef ligature, final/initial forms) and the whole word should be right-aligned. 4. **Console warnings**: GL JS will log a warning if it cannot load a glyph PBF and falls back to the local-font renderer. That’s fine as long as the final visual result is correct. If you see *disconnected* letters or the label rendered left-to-right, double-check: | Possible cause | Fix | |----------------|-----| | Font name typo in `text-font` or `font-faces` | Ensure the string matches exactly the folder name (for glyphs) or the key in `font-faces`. | | CORS error when loading the TTF/OTF | Add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) on the server that hosts the font files. | | Using a glyph server that only contains Latin glyphs | Add the missing Noto Arabic/Hebrew PBFs, or switch to the local-font fallback. | | GL JS version < 6.9.0 and plugin not loaded | Load `setRTLTextPlugin` before `new maplibregl.Map()`. | --- ## 6. Full minimal example (local-font fallback) ```html Arabic & Hebrew RTL labels
``` *Replace the `url` values with the real location of the Noto TTF files you host.* The map will now render Arabic and Hebrew place names correctly, with proper right-to-left joining. --- ## 7. (Optional) Fine-tuning for mixed-script labels If you have labels that contain both RTL and LTR characters (e.g., “مكة (Makkah)”), you can: | Option | How | |--------|-----| | **Force direction per label** | Set `text-direction` to `"right-to-left"` on the layer (as shown). | | **Let the engine decide per-character** | Omit `text-direction` (default `"auto"`). The engine will keep RTL runs right-aligned

Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer**

1. **Upgrade MapLibre GL JS** to **≥ 6.15.0** (the version that draws Devanagari grapheme clusters locally).  
2. **Add a `font-faces` entry** that points to a Devanagari-capable TTF/OTF (e.g. *Noto Sans Devanagari*).  
3. **Make the `text-font` list use the same name** you gave in `font-faces`.  
4. **(Optional) keep the `glyphs` URL** – it will be ignored for Devanagari, but leaving it in place lets the same style work on MapLibre Native.  

That’s all you need; the glyph-PBF server is not used for Devanagari because the glyph format can’t represent the required ligature shaping.

---

## Why the glyph-PBF server breaks Devanagari

| What the style does today | What actually happens |
|---------------------------|-----------------------|
| `glyphs: "https://my-host/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"`  | The map asks the server for a PBF for each Unicode *code-point* (U+0905, U+093F, …). |
| `text-font: ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"]` | The server returns a separate SDF image for every code-point. The GL engine then draws each image **independently**, so vowel signs, diacritics and conjuncts appear as separate floating pieces. |

Devanagari (and other Indic scripts) requires **shaping**: a base consonant + vowel sign = a single glyph, sometimes with complex positioning. The glyph-PBF format cannot express that, so the only reliable way to render it is to let a real text engine (browser or HarfBuzz) do the shaping.

Since **MapLibre GL JS 6.7.0** the engine falls back to the browser’s text layout for any script that has a `font-faces` entry covering the code-points. From **6.15.0** it does this for *every* grapheme cluster, even when a `glyphs` URL is present. The glyph server is therefore ignored for Devanagari, and the text is drawn correctly.

---

## Step-by-step fix

### 1. Use a recent GL JS version

```bash
npm i maplibre-gl@^6.15.0   # or a later version
```

If you load the library from a CDN, point at the newest release:

```html
<script src="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@6.15.0/dist/maplibre-gl.js"></script>
<link href="https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl@6.15.0/dist/maplibre-gl.css" rel="stylesheet" />
```

> **Why?** Versions < 6.7.0 never used the browser for shaping; versions 6.7-6.14 used the browser *only* when a glyph PBF failed to load. 6.15+ always uses the browser for Devanagari (and all other complex scripts) when a matching `font-faces` entry exists.

### 2. Add a `font-faces` entry for Devanagari

In the **root** of your style JSON (same level as `version`, `sources`, `layers`, …) add:

```json
"font-faces": {
  "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
    {
      "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
      "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
    }
  ]
}
```

* **`url`** must be reachable from the browser (CORS-enabled, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or your domain).  
* The **name** (`Noto Sans Devanagari Regular`) must match exactly the string you use in `text-font`.  
* The `unicode-range` is optional but recommended – it tells the engine that this file only covers Devanagari, so other code-points can still fall back to the glyph server.

If you already have a `font-faces` block for other scripts, just add a new entry; you can keep the existing one.

### 3. Reference the font in your symbol layers

```json
{
  "id": "place-labels-hi",
  "type": "symbol",
  "source": "osm",
  "source-layer": "place",
  "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"],
  "layout": {
    "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"],          // Hindi name property
    "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"], // must match font-faces name
    "text-size": 14,
    "text-anchor": "top"
  },
  "paint": {
    "text-color": "#222"
  }
}
```

> **Tip:** Keep the fallback list (e.g. `["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"]`) if you want a generic Latin fallback for any stray Latin characters.

### 4. (Optional) Keep the `glyphs` URL for Native compatibility

MapLibre Native still **requires** a `glyphs` URL for any style that will be rendered on Android/iOS. The presence of `font-faces` does **not** replace it there. So you can leave the field unchanged:

```json
"glyphs": "https://my-host/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf"
```

The native SDK will ignore the Devanagari PBFs (they’re never used) but will still use them for Latin, Cyrillic, etc., and will also read the `font-faces` entries for shaping.

### 5. Verify in the browser console

Open the page, open DevTools → **Network** and filter by **font** or **pbf**. You should see:

* The **TTF/OTF** file requested once (cached thereafter).  
* **No** `…/Noto%20Sans%20Devanagari%20Regular/0-255.pbf` (or any other Devanagari range) requests.  

If you still see glyph-PBF requests for Devanagari ranges, double-check that:

* The `font-faces` name matches exactly (including case and spaces).  
* The `unicode-range` covers the characters you are displaying.  
* You are really running ≥ 6.15.0 (check `maplibregl.version` in the console).

---

## Full minimal style example

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://my-host/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "font-faces": {
    "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "sources": {
    "osm": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://example.com/tileset.json"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    },
    {
      "id": "place-labels-hi",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"],
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"],
        "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"],
        "text-size": 14,
        "text-anchor": "top"
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Load it with:

```js
import maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl';

const map = new maplibregl.Map({
  container: 'map',
  style: 'https://example.com/styles/hindi.json',
  center: [77.2, 28.6],
  zoom: 10
});
```

You should now see Hindi labels with proper vowel-sign placement, conjuncts, and correct line-break behavior.

---

## Common pitfalls & how to diagnose them

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Vowel signs appear **far to the right** of the base consonant | `font-faces` entry missing or name mismatch → GL falls back to glyph-PBFs (one per code-point). | Add correct `font-faces` entry; verify name matches exactly. |
| No Devanagari text at all (labels disappear) | `glyphs` URL unreachable **and** no `font-faces` entry → GL cannot draw anything. | Ensure either a reachable `glyphs` URL **or** a `font-faces` entry. |
| Text looks correct on desktop but wrong on mobile browsers | CORS on the TTF/OTF file blocked on the mobile domain. | Serve the font with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain). |
| You still see many `*.pbf` requests for Devanagari ranges | Running an older GL JS version (< 6.7) or the `font-faces` entry is placed **inside** a layer (invalid location). | Upgrade GL JS; move `font-faces` to the root of the style JSON. |
| Native app shows broken Hindi labels even after the GL JS fix | Native does not yet support the local-font fallback for Devanagari. | Keep the `glyphs` URL **and** add the same `font-faces` entry; Native will use HarfBuzz shaping with the TTF/OTF. |

---

## TL;DR checklist

- [ ] **Upgrade** to MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.15.0.  
- [ ] Add a **root-level `font-faces`** entry that points to a Devanagari TTF/OTF (Noto Sans Devanagari is the easiest).  
- [ ] Use the **exact same name** in every `text-font` that should render Hindi.  
- [ ] Keep the existing `glyphs` URL if you also need the style on Native; it will be ignored for Devanagari on GL JS.  
- [ ] Verify in the network tab that only the TTF/OTF is fetched, not any Devanagari PBFs.  

After those steps, Hindi labels will be shaped correctly, with vowel signs and conjuncts positioned exactly as they appear in native text editors. Happy mapping!
